name: sylph
desc: Ultrafast taxonomic profiling and genome querying for metagenomic samples
why: Metagenomic taxonomic profiling is real science you can run on sequencing data, though the appeal to a general reader is narrow.

brief.what_it_is: Sylph is a command-line tool for taxonomic profiling of metagenomic shotgun reads. It takes sequencing reads from a sample and reports which species are present and their abundances, measured against reference databases such as GTDB (about 200k genomes). It also supports containment ANI querying, where you search a single reference genome against your reads and get an estimated average nucleotide identity for any matching strain. It works with short reads and with nanopore or PacBio long reads.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as fast and precise species-level profiling. It claims to be more than 50x faster than other methods and to have fewer false positives than Kraken, while matching marker-gene methods such as MetaPhlAn and mOTUs on precision and sensitivity.
brief.how_it_works: The docs describe sylph as a k-mer containment method. Its stated novelty is a statistical technique for estimating k-mer containment at low genome coverage, which the authors say gives accurate results for low-abundance organisms. The docs point to a newer database format, syl2db, for more efficient profiling.
brief.install_notes: The README and docs point to sylph-docs.github.io for installation and usage. I did not reach the install or quick-start pages, so I have no install commands. The docs mention pre-built databases for prokaryotes, viruses and eukaryotes, and custom databases built from your own MAGs. Brew installs the executable named sylph.
brief.standout: Rather than relying on marker genes or exact k-mer classification, sylph uses containment with a statistical correction for low coverage. The README also offers ANI estimates for a reference genome down to about 0.1x coverage, which is a different question from 'what species is here'.
brief.status: Appears active. The README has an IMPORTANT notice that documentation moved to sylph-docs.github.io and that GitHub wikis are out of date. The docs include a Tip saying 'Sylph v1 is released September 2026', which I could not check against a release tag. I did not see a last-release or last-commit date, so the exact maintenance state is unknown.
brief.caveats: Documentation lives on an external site, and the GitHub wiki is stale. The README says sylph has 'less false positives than Kraken' and is 'about as precise and sensitive as marker gene methods', which are benchmark claims I did not verify. The docs point to a 'what sylph can and can not do' page that I did not fetch, so its limits are unknown. The docs page I fetched rendered mostly as navigation, so some content may have been missed. The README's 'Sylph v1 is released September 2026' line may be a typo, and I could not confirm the release date. The scout note calls the appeal to a general reader narrow.

entry.title: sylph
entry.tldr: Sylph tells you which microbial species are in a metagenomic sample by comparing k-mers against genome databases, in seconds rather than hours.
entry.deeper_look:
Sylph is a command-line tool for taxonomic profiling of metagenomic shotgun reads. You give it sequencing reads from a sample, such as gut, soil or water, and it reports which species are present and in what proportions. It checks them against reference databases like GTDB, which holds about 200k genomes. It handles short reads and nanopore or PacBio long reads.

The idea underneath is k-mer containment. Instead of classifying every read, or looking only at marker genes, sylph asks how much of a reference genome's k-mer content shows up in the reads. Its stated novelty is a statistical correction for low coverage, so organisms present in small amounts can still be estimated accurately. The README claims it can be more than 50x faster than other methods and produces fewer false positives than Kraken. Those are the authors' benchmark claims, not something checked here.

The same machinery answers a different question. In containment ANI querying, you take one reference genome and search it against your reads. Sylph returns an estimated average nucleotide identity for any matching strain, according to the README down to roughly 0.1x coverage. That is a question about strains, not just which species is present.

The docs also mention a newer database format, syl2db, pre-built databases for prokaryotes, viruses and eukaryotes, and custom databases built from your own assembled genomes.
entry.install:
brew install sylph
# You will need sequencing reads (FASTQ) and a reference database; see sylph-docs.github.io for where to get them.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the subcommands and options so you can see how profiling and querying are split up.

entry.whats_unique: Sylph uses k-mer containment with a statistical correction for low coverage, rather than marker genes or exact k-mer classification. The same method gives strain-level ANI estimates for a single genome at very low coverage.
entry.caveats: Real use needs sequencing data and a large reference database, the documentation lives on a separate site because the GitHub wiki is out of date, and the speed and accuracy claims are the authors' own.
